primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'justice' (Hebrew mishpat/tsedaqah; Greek dikaiosyne) is understood primarily as an essential attribute of God's character and the corresponding moral demand He places on His people: rightly ordered relationships, faithfulness to covenant obligations, impartial judgment, and active protection of the vulnerable (the poor, widow, orphan, and foreigner). It is less a 'symbol' in the strict sense than a core theological concept: justice is the foundation of God's throne and rule, and doing justice is presented as inseparable from genuine worship and knowledge of God. In the New Testament it converges with 'righteousness' (the same Greek word family), so justice is also read as God's saving action to set things right, culminating in Christ.
primary_basis: Micah 6:8 ('do justice, love mercy, walk humbly with your God')
Amos 5:24 ('let justice roll down like waters')
Isaiah 1:17 ('seek justice, correct oppression, bring justice to the fatherless')
Psalm 89:14 / Psalm 97:2 ('righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne')
Deuteronomy 10:17-18 (God executes justice for the fatherless and widow)
Genesis 18:19 (Abraham's household to keep 'righteousness and justice')
Deuteronomy 16:20 ('justice, and only justice, you shall follow')
Jeremiah 22:15-16 (doing justice equated with knowing God)
Isaiah 42:1-4 (the Servant brings forth justice to the nations)
Matthew 23:23 (justice, mercy, faithfulness as 'weightier matters of the law')
Luke 4:18-19 (Jesus' mission to the poor, captives, oppressed, citing Isaiah 61)
Luke 18:1-8 (parable of the persistent widow; God will grant justice)

alternatives.meaning: Retributive/judicial justice: God's righteous judgment and punishment of sin, culminating in final judgment; justice as the demand satisfied at the cross (penal or satisfaction theories of atonement).
basis: Genesis 18:25 ('shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?')

alternatives.meaning: Forensic righteousness/justification: since Greek dikaiosyne covers both 'justice' and 'righteousness,' many (especially Protestant) readings treat justice primarily as the righteous status God imputes or grants to believers through faith in Christ.

Liberationist/social-justice reading: justice as God's preferential concern for the poor and oppressed, mandating structural and political liberation, not only personal ethics (liberation theology, much of Catholic social teaching, and progressive Protestantism).

Justice as God's covenant faithfulness: 'the righteousness/justice of God' read as His faithfulness to His covenant promises to Israel and creation (associated with N.T. Wright and much recent Pauline scholarship).
Classical/Thomistic virtue reading: justice as one of the four cardinal virtues—the settled disposition to render to each person what is due—integrated with natural law in Catholic moral theology.

notes: 'Justice' is a foundational theological concept rather than a figurative symbol like 'lamb' or 'leaven,' so 'symbolic meaning' here means its recognized theological content. There is broad ecumenical consensus on the core: justice is an attribute of God and a covenant demand centered on right relationships and care for the vulnerable (Micah 6:8, Amos 5:24). The main divergences are matters of emphasis—retributive vs. restorative, personal vs. structural, forensic justification vs. social ethics—and often track denominational and political lines. The overlap of 'justice' and 'righteousness' in the underlying Hebrew and Greek vocabulary is the principal source of interpretive variation in English-language discussion.
